name: Aichelburg-Sexl Ultraboost
description: The gravitational field of a massless particle, the Schwarzschild field boosted to the speed of light with its energy held fixed. Spacetime is flat on either side of a single null plane, which carries an impulsive gravitational shock wave with the particle at its centre.
convention: We keep factors of $G$ and $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Richard Tolman, Paul Ehrenfest and Boris Podolsky worked out in 1931 the weak gravitational field of a steady pencil of light and of a passing pulse [tolman1931]. A test ray moving parallel to the pencil keeps the speed of light and feels no gravitational action, while rays moving in any other direction do [tolman1931]. A test particle beside the middle of the pencil is pulled toward it with twice the acceleration Newton's theory would give [tolman1931]. William Bonnor found exact solutions in 1969 for a steady beam of light and for two parallel beams shining the same way, which do not interact [bonnor1969light]. His solutions are gravitational waves with plane wave fronts, of the family Heinrich Brinkmann had found in 1925 [bonnor1969light, brinkmann1925].¶Peter Aichelburg and Roman Sexl asked for the field of a single massless point particle in 1971 [aichelburg1971]. They first solved the linearized field equations, and found their answer identical to an exact solution, which they obtained from the Schwarzschild metric by a singular Lorentz transformation [aichelburg1971]. In the limit the source moves at the speed of light and its mass goes to zero, with its energy $E$ held fixed [aichelburg1971, eardley2002]. The field vanishes everywhere except on the plane through the particle orthogonal to its motion, where the Riemann tensor has a singularity of the delta function type and is of Petrov type N [aichelburg1971]. On that plane the profile obeys Poisson's equation in the two transverse directions with the particle as its point source, which makes it $-(8GE/c^4)\ln(\rho/\rho_0)$ at distance $\rho$ from the particle, with $\rho_0$ any fixed length [eardley2002].¶Impulsive gravitational waves can be built in Minkowski space by cutting it along a null hypersurface and joining the two halves again with a warp, as Roger Penrose did in 1972 [penrose1972impulsive, podolsky1999expanding]. A massless particle moving along the horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole carries a spherical shock wave, which Tevian Dray and Gerard 't Hooft found in 1985 [dray1985]. Aichelburg and Sexl's plane shock and Penrose's sourceless waves both follow from their procedure as special cases [dray1985]. Dray and 't Hooft derived the plane shock a second time by calculating the geodesics that cross it [dray1985]. A geodesic crossing the shock at distance $\rho$ from the particle jumps along it in $v = ct + z$ by $-(8GE/c^4)\ln(\rho/\rho_0)$ and is turned toward the particle [eardley2002]. Boosted the same way, the Kerr-Newman black hole gives a shock carrying charge and spin, the Kerr black hole boosted along its axis the wave of a ring of massless particles, and the Schwarzschild-de Sitter and Schwarzschild-anti-de Sitter black holes shocks with a cosmological constant, as Carlos Lousto and Norma Sánchez, Valeria Ferrari and Paolo Pendenza, and Masahiro Hotta and M. Tanaka found between 1989 and 1993 [lousto1989, ferrari1990, hotta1993].¶At centre of mass energies of the order of the Planck energy and beyond, graviton exchange dominates over every other interaction between two pointlike particles, so that their scattering can be calculated with known laws of physics, as Gerard 't Hooft argued in 1987 [thooft1987]. He expected black holes to form far above the Planck mass, with coherent emission of real gravitons [thooft1987]. Superstrings colliding above Planckian energies scatter mainly by graviton exchange at large impact parameters, as Daniele Amati, Marcello Ciafaloni and Gabriele Veneziano found the same year by resumming string loops to all orders [amati1987]. The exact quantum scattering of a particle by the Aichelburg-Sexl geometry, which Héctor de Vega and Norma Sánchez solved in 1989, gives with a continuous regularisation the phase shift 't Hooft had found in four dimensions [devega1989]. Forward scattering at such energies is described by a topological field theory, as Herman and Erik Verlinde showed in 1992, recovering 't Hooft's results [verlinde1992].¶Two shocks moving head on cannot influence each other until they collide, so the geometry outside the future light cone of the collision is the two single shock solutions superposed [eardley2002]. That geometry holds a closed trapped surface, which Penrose found in unpublished work of 1974, and it bounds the mass of the black hole that forms from below by $1/\sqrt{2}$ of the total energy [eardley2002]. Peter D'Eath and P. N. Payne treated the collision in perturbation theory in 1992, and estimated that $16.4\%$ of the energy leaves as gravitational waves [death1992a, death1992c]. Trapped surfaces form at a nonzero impact parameter too, up to $b_{\max} \approx 3.219\,G\mu/c^4$ for two particles each of energy $\mu$, as Douglas Eardley and Steven Giddings found in 2002 [eardley2002].¶Steven Giddings and Scott Thomas, and Savas Dimopoulos and Greg Landsberg, argued in 2001 that if the fundamental Planck scale lay near a TeV the Large Hadron Collider would produce black holes [giddings2002, dimopoulos2001]. The classical cross section for black hole production is then at least about $65\%$ of the estimate $\pi r_h^2$, with $r_h$ the Schwarzschild radius of the total energy, by Eardley and Giddings's trapped surfaces [eardley2002]. An apparent horizon forms when the impact parameter is less than about $1.5$ times the Schwarzschild radius of the energy of each particle, its effective gravitational radius, as Hirotaka Yoshino and Yasusada Nambu found numerically in 2003 [yoshino2003].¶Ulrich Sperhake, Vitor Cardoso, Frans Pretorius, Emanuele Berti and José A. González collided two black holes head on in 2008, at up to $0.94$ times the speed of light, by solving Einstein's equations numerically [sperhake2008]. Extrapolating to the ultrarelativistic limit, they found that $(14 \pm 3)\%$ of the energy goes into gravitational waves [sperhake2008]. William East and Pretorius collided fluid spheres held together by their own gravity in 2013, at Lorentz factors from $8$ to $12$, with $88$ to $92\%$ of the initial energy in the kinetic energy of their motion, and found that black holes form above a Lorentz factor of $8.5 \pm 0.5$ [east2013]. The threshold they found lies a factor of a few below the estimate of the hoop conjecture, which they traced to each sphere acting as a gravitational lens on the other [east2013]. Those black holes radiate $(16 \pm 2)\%$ of the total energy, close to the $16.4\%$ of D'Eath and Payne [east2013, death1992c].

related.text: The Aichelburg-Sexl shock is a limit of Schwarzschild's field: the boost is taken to the speed of light with the energy held fixed, which flattens the field onto a null plane [aichelburg1971].
The family of waves with plane fronts and parallel rays that Heinrich Brinkmann found in 1925, to which the Aichelburg-Sexl shock belongs [brinkmann1925, bonnor1969light].
Flat spacetime on either side of the shock. Roger Penrose built such waves in 1972 by cutting Minkowski space along a null plane and joining the halves again with a warp [penrose1972impulsive].
A steady beam of light of finite width, whose exact field William Bonnor found in 1969. Outside the beam its profile is the shock's logarithm with no delta in front [bonnor1969light].
Another pp-wave whose profile is harmonic off a line. Here the line is the path of a massless particle, there a cosmic string carrying a wave [garfinkle1990].
The rotating black hole, boosted the same way. Valeria Ferrari and Paolo Pendenza took the limit along its axis in 1990 and found the field of massless particles on a ring [ferrari1990].

Two impulsive waves colliding, each with a plane front of the same strength everywhere, which focus each other onto a singularity [khan1971]. Two Aichelburg-Sexl shocks meeting head on close a trapped surface around the collision, as Penrose found in 1974 [eardley2002].
The counterparts of the pp-waves in anti-de Sitter space. Squeezed onto one front, a Siklos wave is the field of a null particle there [podolsky1998impulsive].
A black string moving around a small fifth dimension is a charged black hole to four dimensions. At the speed of light it is a wave of this kind in five dimensions [horowitz2012].

Aichelburg and Sexl's boost done to the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole. Its shock is a sphere of fixed area on a cosmological horizon, and this plane is its limit as the cosmological constant goes to zero [hotta1993, podolsky1999nonexpanding].
The same mass boosted past the speed of light. The field of that tachyon is two of Ehlers and Kundt's metrics, A II inside a cone of shock and B I outside it [hruska2019].

coordinates.name: Cartesian

parameters.description: Energy of the massless source, the limit of $Mc^2/\sqrt{1 - V^2/c^2}$ as its rest mass $M$ goes to zero and its speed $V$ to $c$
An arbitrary length; changing it moves $v$ behind the shock by a constant, which is a change of coordinates

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta, a prime on it a derivative with respect to its argument. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 - \dfrac{4GE}{c^4}\ln\left(\dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{\rho_0^2}\right)\delta(ct - z)\left(c\,dt - dz\right)^2

coordinates.name: Null Cartesian

parameters.description: Energy of the massless source, the limit of $Mc^2/\sqrt{1 - V^2/c^2}$ as its rest mass $M$ goes to zero and its speed $V$ to $c$
An arbitrary length; changing it moves $v$ behind the shock by a constant, which is a change of coordinates

coordinates.convention: We use the null coordinates $u = ct - z$ and $v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $x$ and $y$ the transverse lengths, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta, a prime on it a derivative with respect to its argument. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.convention: We use the null coordinates $u = ct - z$ and $v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $\rho$ the distance from the axis of the source and $\phi$ the angle about it, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta, a prime on it a derivative with respect to its argument.
